subject: ss
title: U.S. History I: Colonies to the Civil War
objectives: You will place major events from 1607 to 1865 in chronological order and explain cause-and-effect links between them.
You will explain why the colonies declared independence, using the principle of no taxation without representation.
You will describe key precedents and policies of the early republic, including Washington's Farewell Address and the Monroe Doctrine.
You will explain how westward expansion and the question of slavery in the territories increased sectionalism and led to the Civil War.
You will interpret public-domain documents, timelines, and data about this period to answer GED-style questions.

slides.title: U.S. History I: Colonies to the Civil War
slides.board:
Week 5 Social Studies: U.S. History I, 1607–1865

Today you will:

  • Put major events from Jamestown to Appomattox in order and link causes to effects
  • Explain why the colonies broke with Britain: "no taxation without representation"
  • Describe the precedents and policies of the early republic
  • Explain how westward expansion and slavery led to the Civil War
  • Answer GED-style questions with documents, timelines, and data

Plan: Warm-up → six eras → we do it together → you do it → GED questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 5. U.S. history is about one-fifth of the GED Social Studies test, and today we cover the first half of the story: from the first English colony in 1607 to the end of the Civil War in 1865. You will not need to memorize hundreds of dates. You need the big story in the right order, and you need to read old documents and charts carefully. Our anchor rule for the whole lesson: causes come before effects.
ask: What do you already know about why the American colonies broke away from Britain? (Expected: any answer, such as taxes or the Boston Tea Party. Tell the student we will build on whatever they said.)

slides.title: Warm-up: Last Week in Review
slides.board:
Week 4 review: Government in Action.

  1. A state has 9 members in the House of Representatives. How many electoral votes does it have?
  2. Party or interest group? A nurses' association meets with senators to support a hospital staffing bill. It does not run candidates.
  3. The president vetoes a bill. The House votes 300–130 to override; the Senate votes 64–36. Does the bill become law?
  4. Congress adjourns 4 days after sending a bill to the president, who never signs it. What happens?
steps: 1. 9 House members + 2 senators = 11 electoral votes.
2. Interest group. It lobbies lawmakers but does not nominate or run candidates.
3. No. House: 300 of 430 ≈ 70%, which passes two-thirds. Senate: 64 of 100 = 64%, short of two-thirds (67 needed with all 100 voting). Both chambers must reach two-thirds.
4. The bill dies. This is a pocket veto: Congress adjourned before the 10 days (Sundays excepted) ran out.

notes.say: Before we go back in time, let us make sure last week's civics is solid, because it shows up on every practice test. Give the student about three minutes for all four, then have them tell you each answer and the reason before you reveal it. Question 3 is the one most people miss, so ask for the math out loud.
ask: Why does every state get at least 3 electoral votes? (Expected: every state has at least 1 House member plus 2 senators)

What is the difference between a regular veto and a pocket veto? (Expected: a regular veto can be overridden by two-thirds of both chambers; a pocket veto happens when Congress adjourns and the president does nothing, and it cannot be overridden)
notes.answer: 1. 11. 2. Interest group. 3. No: the Senate vote (64%) is short of two-thirds. 4. The bill dies (pocket veto).
notes.watch: On question 3, students often stop after the House. Remind them: an override needs two-thirds in both chambers. One short chamber kills it.

slides.title: Era 1: The Colonial Era, 1607–1763
slides.board:
YearEventWhy it matters
1607Jamestown, VirginiaFirst permanent English settlement; tobacco made it pay
1619House of Burgesses; first recorded Africans in VirginiaFirst elected assembly; beginning of slavery in the colonies
1620Mayflower CompactSelf-government by agreement

Three regions: New England (fishing, shipbuilding, trade) · Middle (grain, "breadbasket") · Southern (plantations, enslaved labor)

Mercantilism: colonies send raw materials to England and buy English goods.

notes.say: England's first permanent settlement was Jamestown, Virginia, in 1607. It nearly failed until colonists learned to grow tobacco for sale in England. In 1619 two things happened in Virginia that shaped the whole story: the House of Burgesses met, the first elected assembly in the English colonies, and the first recorded Africans arrived, the beginning of a system that grew into slavery. In 1620 the Pilgrims signed the Mayflower Compact, agreeing to make and obey their own laws. So from the very start, the colonies had two threads: self-government and slavery. Geography shaped three regions, and Britain ran the whole system under mercantilism, which means the colonies existed to make the home country rich.
ask: Which two things that began in Virginia in 1619 pull in opposite directions? (Expected: the House of Burgesses, which is self-government, and the arrival of enslaved Africans, which is the beginning of slavery)
Why did New England rely on fishing and trade instead of big farms? (Expected: rocky soil and cold winters)
notes.watch: Students often place Jamestown in New England because it was so early. Jamestown is in Virginia, a Southern colony. The Pilgrims came to New England later, in 1620.

slides.title: Worked Example: Who Benefits?
slides.board:
Under the Navigation Acts, a Virginia planter may ship his tobacco only to England. He must buy his tools and cloth from English merchants, and goods from France must pass through an English port first.

Which economic system does this describe, and which country benefits most?
steps: Find the pattern. Raw material (tobacco) goes to England; finished goods (tools, cloth) come from England.
Find the rule. Trade must pass through England, even trade with France.
Name the system. Colonies supply raw materials and buy the home country's goods: mercantilism.
Who benefits? England: its merchants, shippers, and treasury profit at each step. Later, rules like these fed colonial anger at British control of trade.

notes.say: Model the thinking: follow the goods. Draw two arrows on the board, raw materials going to England and finished goods coming back. When every arrow runs through the home country, you are looking at mercantilism. Then connect it forward: when Britain later tightened its control over colonial trade and added taxes, colonists already resented being managed for England's benefit.
ask: If the planter could sell tobacco directly to France, would that fit mercantilism? (Expected: No; mercantilism routes trade through the home country)
notes.watch: Students sometimes say "capitalism" or "free trade." Ask: "Is the planter free to sell wherever he wants?" No: the law forces trade through England.

slides.title: Era 2: The Road to Revolution, 1763–1783
slides.board:
The chain: war debt → new taxes → protest → punishment → war → independence

YearEvent
1754–1763French and Indian War leaves Britain in debt
1765Stamp Act → "No taxation without representation"; boycotts
1773 → 1774Boston Tea Party → Coercive Acts close Boston Harbor
1775Fighting at Lexington and Concord
1776Declaration of Independence (July 4)
1777 → 1778Victory at Saratoga → France becomes an ally
1781 → 1783British surrender at Yorktown → Treaty of Paris

notes.say: Britain won the French and Indian War in 1763 but was deep in debt, partly from defending the colonies. Parliament decided the colonists should help pay, so it passed taxes like the Stamp Act in 1765. The colonists' objection was not mainly the amount. It was the principle: they elected no one to Parliament, so Parliament had no right to tax them. That is "no taxation without representation." Each British action brought a colonial protest, and each protest brought a harsher British response, until fighting broke out at Lexington and Concord in 1775. The Declaration followed in 1776, the win at Saratoga brought France into the war, and Yorktown in 1781 effectively ended the fighting.
ask: Why did Britain start taxing the colonies after 1763? (Expected: to pay debts from the French and Indian War and the cost of defending the colonies)
Was the colonists' main complaint the size of the tax? (Expected: No; it was that they had no representatives in Parliament to consent to it)
notes.watch: Students mix up the Declaration (1776) and the Constitution (1787). Ask: "Does this document break away, or build a government?" The Declaration breaks away.

slides.title: Worked Example: Which Event Was the Response?
slides.board:
Timeline:

  • 1763: Proclamation of 1763 bans settlement west of the Appalachians.
  • 1765: Stamp Act taxes newspapers and legal papers.
  • 1765: Colonists boycott British goods.
  • 1766: Parliament repeals the Stamp Act.

Which event was a direct response to the Stamp Act? What was the effect of that response?
steps: Anchor the cause: the Stamp Act, 1765. A response must come after it.
Eliminate: the Proclamation (1763) came first, so it cannot be a response.
Find the action against the tax: the colonists' boycott of British goods (1765).
Follow the chain: British merchants lost sales, and Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766. Cause → response → result.

notes.say: This is the single most common history format on the GED: a timeline and a "which event led to" question. Say the rule out loud: effects never come before causes. Then show the student that one event can be both: the boycott is an effect of the Stamp Act and a cause of the repeal. History is a chain, not a list.
ask: Was the boycott a cause or an effect? (Expected: both; it was caused by the Stamp Act and helped cause the repeal)
notes.watch: Some students pick the Proclamation of 1763 because it is also a British action the colonists disliked. Point to the dates: 1763 is before 1765.

slides.title: We Do: Put It in Order and Find the Link
slides.board:
Put these five events in order. Then answer the question.

  • Treaty of Paris recognizes independence
  • Declaration of Independence
  • France signs an alliance with the United States
  • Battle of Saratoga
  • British surrender at Yorktown

Which event most directly led France to join the war?
steps: 1st: Declaration of Independence (1776)
2nd: Battle of Saratoga (1777)
3rd: French alliance (1778)
4th: Yorktown (1781), then 5th: Treaty of Paris (1783)
The link: the American victory at Saratoga convinced France the Americans could win, so France joined as an ally.

notes.say: Now we do one together. Have the student place each event before you reveal it, and ask for a reason, not just a guess. Even without exact dates, logic helps: you declare independence before you fight for allies, the surrender comes before the peace treaty, and an ally joins after you prove you can win.
ask: Why would France wait until after Saratoga to join? (Expected: France wanted proof the Americans could win before risking war with Britain)
Which comes first, the surrender at Yorktown or the peace treaty? Why? (Expected: Yorktown; the fighting ends, then the countries negotiate the treaty)
notes.answer: Order: Declaration (1776), Saratoga (1777), French alliance (1778), Yorktown (1781), Treaty of Paris (1783). Saratoga led France to join.
notes.watch: Students often think the war ended in 1776 with the Declaration. Stress that declaring independence and winning it are different: the war went on until 1781, and the treaty came in 1783.

slides.title: Era 3: The Early Republic, 1781–1824
slides.board:
• Articles of Confederation (1781): weak national government, no power to tax
  • Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787) → leaders write the Constitution (1787)
  • Washington (1789–1797) sets precedents: a cabinet, two terms, neutrality
  • Hamilton vs. Jefferson → first political parties
  • 1800: power passes peacefully between parties
  • Louisiana Purchase (1803, from France): nation roughly doubles
  • War of 1812 with Britain: a draw, but national pride
  • Monroe Doctrine (1823): no new European colonies in the Americas

notes.say: Winning independence was one problem; governing was another. The first plan, the Articles of Confederation, made the national government so weak it could not collect taxes or pay its soldiers. When farmers in Massachusetts rebelled in Shays' Rebellion, many leaders decided a stronger government was needed, and they wrote the Constitution in 1787. George Washington then set precedents, examples later presidents followed, such as serving only two terms. In foreign policy, the early republic had one big theme: stay out of Europe's wars and keep Europe out of the Americas. Washington said it in 1796, Jefferson repeated it in 1801, and Monroe extended it in 1823.
ask: What is a precedent? Give one Washington set. (Expected: an example later leaders follow; serving only two terms, or forming a cabinet)
Why did Shays' Rebellion matter? (Expected: it showed the Articles government was too weak and pushed leaders to write the Constitution)
notes.watch: Students think the Constitution came right after independence. The Articles came first (1781), and the Constitution replaced them because they failed.

slides.title: Worked Example: Decode Washington
slides.board:
"I have already intimated to you the danger of parties in the State, with particular reference to the founding of them on geographical discriminations. Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally."

(George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796)

What is Washington warning against?
steps: Translate the hard words: intimated = hinted; parties = political factions; geographical discriminations = divisions by region; baneful = harmful.
Sentence 1 in plain English: I already warned you that parties are dangerous, especially parties based on region.
Sentence 2 in plain English: Now I warn you, very seriously, that party spirit in general is harmful.
Answer: Washington warns that political parties, especially parties based on region, could harm the nation. Look ahead: regional parties are exactly what split the country in the 1850s.

notes.say: Old documents look hard because of a few unfamiliar words. Model the method: underline the hard words, translate each one, then rewrite each sentence in plain English. Only then answer. Notice the payoff: Washington's fear of parties built on geography is a preview of the North-South split we study later today.
ask: Which phrase tells you he is especially worried about regional parties? (Expected: "geographical discriminations")
notes.watch: Watch for students who say Washington warned against "entangling alliances." That phrase is Jefferson's (1801). Washington said "permanent alliances." On the GED, use the exact words in the excerpt.

slides.title: We Do: Read the Monroe Doctrine
slides.board:
"…the American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers.… Our policy in regard to Europe… remains the same, which is, not to interfere in the internal concerns of any of its powers…"

(James Monroe, Annual Message to Congress, 1823)

  1. What does Monroe tell Europe not to do?
  2. What does he promise the United States will not do?
  3. How does this build on Washington's advice?
steps: 1. Europe must not create new colonies in North or South America ("not… subjects for future colonization").
2. The United States will not interfere in Europe's internal affairs.
3. Washington said stay out of Europe's politics. Monroe keeps that and adds the other direction: Europe must stay out of the Americas. Separation now runs both ways.

notes.say: Read the excerpt aloud with the student, phrase by phrase. Have them rewrite "subjects for future colonization" in their own words before answering. Then ask them to compare it with Washington. This "how does document B relate to document A" question is a GED favorite.
ask: What does "henceforth" mean? (Expected: from now on)
Does Monroe say Europe must give up the colonies it already has? (Expected: No; he says "future colonization")
notes.answer: 1. Stop creating new colonies in the Americas. 2. Stay out of Europe's internal affairs. 3. It extends Washington's policy of separation in both directions.
notes.watch: Students sometimes say Monroe ordered Europe out of the Americas entirely. The word "future" matters: existing colonies were not the target.

slides.title: Era 4: Westward Expansion, 1803–1853
slides.board:
Manifest Destiny (1845): the belief that the United States was meant to spread to the Pacific.

AdditionYearFrom
Louisiana Purchase1803France
Florida1819Spain
Texas1845Republic of Texas
Oregon1846Great Britain
Mexican Cession1848Mexico (after war)

The cost: Indian Removal Act (1830) → Trail of Tears (1838–1839).
The question every new territory raised: Will slavery be allowed there?

notes.say: In 1845 a journalist named John L. O'Sullivan wrote that it was America's "manifest destiny" to spread across the continent, and the phrase stuck. In fifty years the country added Louisiana, Florida, Texas, Oregon, and the huge Mexican Cession that included California. This expansion came at a terrible cost to Native Americans. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 led to the forced removal of southeastern nations, and thousands of Cherokee died on the Trail of Tears. And every single new territory forced the same argument in Congress: would slavery be allowed there? That question is the bridge from expansion to the Civil War.
ask: Why did every new territory cause an argument between North and South? (Expected: each one raised the question of whether slavery would spread there, which would change the balance of power in Congress)
Which addition came from a war? (Expected: the Mexican Cession, after the Mexican-American War)
notes.watch: Do not let expansion become a simple success story. The GED asks about its effects on Native Americans and Mexico as well as on the United States. Ask: "Who gained, and who lost?"

slides.title: Worked Example: Test a Claim With a Table
slides.board:
AdditionArea (thousand sq. mi.)
Louisiana Purchase (1803)828
Texas (1845)389
Mexican Cession (1848)529

Claim: "The Louisiana Purchase added more land than Texas and the Mexican Cession combined." Is the claim supported?
steps: What does the claim compare? Louisiana alone vs. Texas + Mexican Cession together.
Add: 389 + 529 = 918 thousand square miles.
Compare: 828 < 918. Louisiana is smaller than the two combined.
Answer: Not supported. Louisiana was the largest single addition, but Texas and the Mexican Cession together added about 90 thousand square miles more.

notes.say: On a data question, do the math before you choose. First say exactly what the claim compares, because "combined" changes everything. Many students see that Louisiana has the biggest number in the table and stop there. The claim is not about the biggest single addition; it is about one addition against two others added together.
ask: Which claim would the table support? (Expected: for example, "The Louisiana Purchase was larger than any other single addition in the table")
notes.watch: Students who answer "supported" are reading the largest number instead of the claim. Make them underline the word "combined."

slides.title: Era 5: Sectionalism and Failed Compromises, 1820–1860
slides.board:
Sectionalism = loyalty to your region over the nation. North: factories, cities, free labor. South: cotton grown by enslaved people.

YearEventWhat it did
1820Missouri CompromiseMissouri slave, Maine free; no slavery north of 36°30′ in Louisiana Territory
1850Compromise of 1850California free; stricter Fugitive Slave Act
1854Kansas-Nebraska ActSettlers vote on slavery (popular sovereignty) → "Bleeding Kansas"
1857Dred Scott decisionCongress cannot ban slavery in territories
1860Lincoln electedSouthern states begin to secede

notes.say: The cotton gin, invented in 1793, made cotton enormously profitable, and the South's economy came to depend on cotton grown by enslaved people. The North built factories and railroads. As the country grew, each side feared the other would control Congress. For forty years leaders tried to settle the slavery question with compromises, and each one broke down. The Missouri Compromise drew a line. The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state but forced Northerners to help return people who escaped slavery. The Kansas-Nebraska Act let settlers vote, which led to violence. Then the Supreme Court said in Dred Scott that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories at all. When Lincoln, whose party opposed the spread of slavery, won in 1860, Southern states began to leave the Union.
ask: What does sectionalism mean? (Expected: loyalty to one's own region over the nation as a whole)
Which event undid the Missouri Compromise line in Kansas and Nebraska? (Expected: the Kansas-Nebraska Act, 1854; then Dred Scott in 1857 declared the line unconstitutional)
notes.watch: Students sometimes treat "states' rights" as a separate cause from slavery. In the 1850s the states' rights argument was mainly about protecting slavery. Keep the focus on evidence from the documents.

slides.title: Worked Example: Why Pair Missouri and Maine?
slides.board:
In 1819 the Union had 11 free states and 11 slave states. Each state has 2 senators. Missouri asked to join as a slave state.

Why did Congress admit Maine as a free state at the same time?
steps: Before: 11 free, 11 slave. Senate: 22 free-state senators and 22 slave-state senators. Balanced.
Missouri alone: 11 free, 12 slave. Senate: 22 vs. 24. The slave states would control the Senate.
Missouri and Maine: 12 free, 12 slave. Senate: 24 vs. 24. Balanced again.
Answer: Pairing them kept the balance in the Senate, so neither section could control it.

notes.say: Walk through the arithmetic slowly. The North already had more people, so it controlled the House, where seats depend on population. The Senate, with two senators per state, was where the South could protect slavery. That is why every new state mattered so much. Keep this picture in mind: when California joined as a free state in 1850 without a slave-state partner, the balance tipped for good.
ask: Why was the Senate the key chamber for the South? (Expected: every state gets two senators no matter its population, so equal numbers of slave and free states meant equal power)
notes.watch: Students may think the Missouri Compromise ended slavery somewhere it already existed. It only set rules for new territory: no slavery north of 36°30′ in the rest of the Louisiana Territory.

slides.title: We Do: Trace the Thread
slides.board:
Who decides about slavery in new territory?

  1. 1820, Missouri Compromise: who decided?
  2. 1854, Kansas-Nebraska Act: who decided? Why did this lead to violence?
  3. 1857, Dred Scott: what did the Supreme Court say about Congress's power?
  4. Why did each answer make Northerners or Southerners angrier?
steps: 1. Congress decided, by drawing the 36°30′ line.
2. The settlers decided by vote (popular sovereignty). Both sides rushed settlers into Kansas to win the vote, and armed clashes followed: "Bleeding Kansas."
3. Congress could not ban slavery in the territories; the Missouri Compromise line was unconstitutional.
4. Each change opened more land to slavery. Northerners saw slavery spreading; many joined the new Republican Party (1854) to stop it. Southerners feared any limit on slavery.

notes.say: This is the thread that ties the 1850s together: who gets to decide about slavery in new land? Ask each question and let the student answer before revealing. The pattern they should see is that each "solution" moved the decision and made the conflict worse, not better.
ask: If settlers vote, what is the fastest way to win? (Expected: send more of your own settlers)
After Dred Scott, could Congress stop slavery from spreading? (Expected: No, according to the Court)
notes.answer: 1. Congress. 2. The settlers, by vote; rival settlers fought. 3. Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. 4. Each opened more land to slavery, angering the North; Southern fears grew with every attempt to limit it.
notes.watch: Students may think popular sovereignty means the whole nation voted. It meant only the settlers of that territory.

slides.title: Era 6: The Civil War, 1861–1865
slides.board:
DateEvent
Dec. 1860South Carolina secedes; 11 states form the Confederacy
Apr. 1861Confederates fire on Fort Sumter: war begins
Jan. 1, 1863Emancipation Proclamation
July 1863Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg: turning point
Apr. 1865Lee surrenders at Appomattox Court House
Dec. 1865Thirteenth Amendment abolishes slavery nationwide

Union advantages (1860): about 22 million people vs. 9 million; about 22,000 vs. 9,000 miles of railroad.

notes.say: After Lincoln won in 1860, South Carolina seceded, and eventually eleven states formed the Confederacy. The war began when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861. The North had far more people, factories, and railroads, but the South fought on home ground and only had to defend. On January 1, 1863, Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people in the areas in rebellion and opened the Union army to Black soldiers; about 180,000 served. That July, victories at Gettysburg and Vicksburg turned the war. Lee surrendered at Appomattox in April 1865, and the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery everywhere in the country that December. More than 600,000 soldiers died.
ask: Why did railroads matter so much in this war? (Expected: they moved troops and supplies quickly)
Which ended slavery everywhere: the Emancipation Proclamation or the Thirteenth Amendment? (Expected: the Thirteenth Amendment)
notes.watch: The most common error in this era: thinking the Emancipation Proclamation freed every enslaved person. It applied only to areas in rebellion. Slavery in loyal border states such as Kentucky ended with the Thirteenth Amendment.

slides.title: Worked Example: Who Did the Proclamation Free?
slides.board:
"…all persons held as slaves within any State or designated part of a State, the people whereof shall then be in rebellion against the United States, shall be then, thenceforward, and forever free…"

(Emancipation Proclamation, effective January 1, 1863)

Did this order free enslaved people in Kentucky, a slave state that stayed loyal to the Union?
steps: Find the condition: it applies to states or areas whose people are "in rebellion against the United States."
Test Kentucky: Kentucky stayed in the Union. It was not in rebellion.
Conclusion: The Proclamation did not free enslaved people in Kentucky.
What did? The Thirteenth Amendment (ratified December 1865) abolished slavery everywhere in the United States.

notes.say: Teach the student to find the condition in a legal sentence: the word "whereof" introduces it. Lincoln issued the Proclamation as a war measure under his power as commander in chief, so it reached only the areas fighting against the Union. He did not want to push the loyal border states toward the Confederacy. That is why a constitutional amendment was needed to end slavery everywhere.
ask: Why might Lincoln have left the border states out? (Expected: to keep them loyal to the Union; his war power applied to areas in rebellion)
notes.watch: If the student says yes, ask: "Was Kentucky in rebellion?" Make them point to the condition in the text.

slides.title: You Do 1: Colonies and Revolution
slides.board:
On your own (3 minutes).

  1. Which came first: the Boston Tea Party or the Coercive Acts? Which caused the other?
  2. Name the first elected assembly in the English colonies and its year.
  3. Why did colonists object to the Stamp Act even though the tax was small?
  4. Which victory persuaded France to join the American side?
steps: 1. The Tea Party (1773) came first; Britain passed the Coercive Acts (1774) to punish Boston. 2. The House of Burgesses, 1619. 3. They had no elected representatives in Parliament, so they said Parliament had no right to tax them. 4. Saratoga (1777).

notes.say: Start a three-minute timer and stay quiet. When time is up, have the student give all four answers before you reveal. For question 3, push for the principle, not just "taxes were unfair."
ask: For number 3, what is the four-word slogan? (Expected: no taxation without representation)
notes.answer: 1. Tea Party (1773) caused the Coercive Acts (1774). 2. House of Burgesses, 1619. 3. Taxation without representation; no consent. 4. Saratoga.

slides.title: You Do 2: The Early Republic and Expansion
slides.board:
On your own (3 minutes).

  1. What was the main weakness of the Articles of Confederation?
  2. Washington advised "extending our commercial relations" with foreign nations but having "as little political connection as possible." In plain English?
  3. From which country did the United States buy Louisiana in 1803?
  4. Florida added 72 thousand square miles and Oregon added 286 thousand. How many thousand square miles did they add together?
steps: 1. The national government could not collect taxes (it was too weak). 2. Trade with other nations, but avoid political ties and permanent alliances. 3. France. 4. 72 + 286 = 358 thousand square miles.

notes.say: Timer on: three minutes. When time is up, collect all four answers. On number 2, the student should name both halves: yes to trade, no to political ties. Answers that say "stay away from other countries completely" miss the first half.
ask: For number 2, does Washington want more trade or less? (Expected: more; "extending" means increasing)
notes.answer: 1. It could not tax. 2. Trade, but no permanent political alliances. 3. France. 4. 358 thousand square miles.

slides.title: You Do 3: Sectionalism and the Civil War
slides.board:
On your own (4 minutes).

  1. Put in order: Dred Scott decision; Missouri Compromise; Kansas-Nebraska Act; Compromise of 1850.
  2. What is popular sovereignty?
  3. What event started the Civil War, and in what year?
  4. The Union had about 22,000 miles of railroad; the Confederacy had about 9,000. About how many times as much did the Union have? Round to the nearest tenth.
steps: 1. Missouri Compromise (1820), Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), Dred Scott (1857). 2. Letting the settlers of a territory vote on whether to allow slavery. 3. The Confederate attack on Fort Sumter, 1861. 4. 22,000 ÷ 9,000 ≈ 2.4 times.

notes.say: Four minutes this time, because number 4 needs a calculation. Let the student use a calculator, as they could on the GED Social Studies test. When time is up, collect all four answers, then reveal.
ask: For number 4, which number do you divide by? (Expected: the Confederacy's 9,000, because we want the Union's as a multiple of it)
notes.answer: 1. 1820, 1850, 1854, 1857. 2. Settlers vote on slavery. 3. Fort Sumter, 1861. 4. About 2.4 times.
notes.watch: On number 4, students who divide 9,000 by 22,000 get about 0.4. Ask: "Should the Union's number be bigger or smaller than 1 times the Confederacy's?"

slides.title: GED Question 1: A Speech Before the War
slides.board:
"A house divided against itself cannot stand. I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free. I do not expect the Union to be dissolved—I do not expect the house to fall—but I do expect it will cease to be divided." (Abraham Lincoln, 1858)

Which statement best summarizes Lincoln's point?

A. The Southern states should be allowed to leave the Union peacefully.
B. The nation could not last forever with slavery legal in some states and banned in others.
C. Slavery should be ended immediately by an amendment to the Constitution.
D. The Union would soon break apart into two separate countries.
steps: Eliminate A. Lincoln says "I do not expect the Union to be dissolved." He is not inviting the South to leave.
Eliminate C. The excerpt never mentions an amendment or a timetable. That is outside knowledge about 1865, not this 1858 speech.
Eliminate D. This reverses the text: "I do not expect the house to fall."
Answer B. "Cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free" means the divided nation could not last forever.

notes.say: Show the student how to beat a document question: decode the metaphor first. The "house" is the nation, and "divided" means half slave and half free. Then eliminate out loud with a reason for each. Notice the GED's favorite distractor types here: a reversal of the text and a true-sounding fact from a later time.
ask: What does the "house" stand for? (Expected: the United States, the Union)
Which words prove B? (Expected: "cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free")
notes.answer: B. The nation could not last forever with slavery legal in some states and banned in others.
notes.watch: Students who choose C know that slavery ended by amendment and bring that in. Ask: "Where does the excerpt mention an amendment?"

Answer A is the classic overreach: a real advantage turned into a certainty. Answer D needs a quick calculation, so model it: 3.5 divided by 9 is about 0.39.

What percent of the Confederacy's population was enslaved? (Expected: about 39%)

slides.title: GED Strategy: Anchor the Date
slides.board:
1. Anchor: write the year (or era) of the excerpt or event on your scratch paper.
  2. Cross out the future: an effect can never come before its cause. Any answer about something that had not happened yet is wrong.
  3. Decode old words in plain English before answering.
  4. Stay inside the evidence: eliminate outside knowledge, reversals, and words like certain, all, proves.
  5. Do the math before choosing on a data question.

Pace: about 2 minutes per question.

notes.say: History questions often hide a timing trap. A question about a 1765 document may offer an answer about the Constitution, which did not exist until 1787. If the student anchors the date first, those choices fall away immediately, often leaving only two. Practice this on every question this week until it becomes automatic.
ask: An excerpt is from 1858. Can the correct answer describe the Emancipation Proclamation as a cause of the author's ideas? (Expected: No; the Proclamation came in 1863, after the excerpt)
notes.watch: Strong students sometimes answer from what they know happened later. Ask every time: "Had that happened yet?"

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
About one-fifth of the GED Social Studies test covers U.S. history. You will not need to memorize hundreds of dates. You will need to know the big story, put events in the right order, and read old documents and charts carefully. This lesson covers the first half of that story: from the first English colony in 1607 to the end of the Civil War in 1865.

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Put major events from 1607 to 1865 in order and explain how one event led to the next
  • Explain why the colonies broke with Great Britain, using the idea of "no taxation without representation"
  • Describe the precedents and policies of the early republic, including Washington's Farewell Address and the Monroe Doctrine
  • Explain how westward expansion and the question of slavery led to the Civil War
  • Answer GED-style questions using documents, timelines, and data

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Answer it before you move on.

screens.title: The Big Timeline: Six Eras
screens.html:
Before the details, learn the shape of the whole story. Every event in this lesson fits into one of six eras.

EraYearsBig idea
Colonial era1607–1763English colonies grow; self-government and slavery both begin
Revolution1763–1783British taxes lead to protest, war, and independence
Early republic1781–1824A new government is built and tested
Westward expansion1803–1853The nation grows to the Pacific
Sectionalism1820–1860North and South split over slavery in new land
Civil War1861–1865The Union is saved and slavery is abolished

Key rule: Causes come before effects. When a question asks what led to an event, look only at events that happened earlier.

check.prompt: Drag each event into the correct position, from earliest (1st) to latest (4th).
check.why: The most common mistake is placing the Louisiana Purchase before the Declaration. The United States had to exist (1776) before it could buy land (1803).
check.hint: Which era does each event belong to? Put the eras in order first.
check.explain: Jamestown (1607) → Declaration of Independence (1776) → Louisiana Purchase (1803) → Civil War begins (1861). Use the eras: colonial, revolution, early republic, Civil War.

screens.title: The Colonial Era: Self-Government and Slavery Begin
screens.html:
England's first permanent settlement was Jamestown, Virginia, founded in 1607. It survived because colonists learned to grow tobacco and sell it in England.

Two things happened in Virginia in 1619 that pulled in opposite directions. The House of Burgesses met, the first elected assembly in the English colonies. The same year, the first recorded Africans arrived in Virginia, the beginning of a system that grew into slavery.

In 1620 the Pilgrims signed the Mayflower Compact before landing in Massachusetts. They agreed to form a "civil body politic" and to obey laws made "for the general good of the colony." In 1639 Connecticut settlers adopted the Fundamental Orders, a written plan under which voters elected a governor every year.

These are early examples of self-government: people making their own laws and choosing their own leaders.

check.prompt: The Pilgrims agreed to "combine ourselves together into a civil body politic" and to obey laws made "for the general good of the colony." Which idea does the Mayflower Compact show?
options: Self-government by the agreement of the settlers
Rule by a king who holds unlimited power
Separation of powers among three branches
A plan to declare independence from England
why: The settlers make laws for themselves by agreement. Nothing in the quotation gives a king power over their local laws.
Separation of powers comes from the U.S. Constitution, written in 1787. The Compact says nothing about branches.
The Pilgrims in 1620 still considered themselves English subjects. Independence was not declared until 1776.
check.hint: Who agrees to make the laws in this quotation?
check.explain: The settlers "combine ourselves together" and promise to obey laws made "for the general good." People agreeing to create and obey their own laws is self-government. Separation of powers is a later Constitution idea, and independence did not come until 1776.

screens.title: Three Colonial Regions and Mercantilism
screens.html:
Geography shaped how people lived in the thirteen colonies.

RegionLand and climateEconomy
New EnglandRocky soil, cold wintersFishing, shipbuilding, trade, small farms
MiddleFertile land, milder climateWheat and grain ("breadbasket"), busy ports
SouthernLong, warm growing seasonPlantations of tobacco, rice, indigo using enslaved labor

Britain ran its colonies under mercantilism. In this system, colonies exist to make the home country rich: they send raw materials (tobacco, lumber, furs) to the home country and buy its finished goods (cloth, tools). Laws called the Navigation Acts required much colonial trade to pass through England.

example.prompt: A Virginia planter must ship his tobacco only to England, and he must buy English cloth. Who benefits most?
steps: Raw material (tobacco) goes to England; finished goods (cloth) come back from England.
Every trade passes through England, so English merchants and the English government profit.

check.prompt: Which situation is the best example of mercantilism?
options: A colony must sell its lumber only to the home country and buy that country’s manufactured tools.
A colony may sell its lumber to any country that offers the highest price for it.
A colony elects an assembly that passes laws for the colonists who live there.
A colony bans all trade so its people must produce everything they need.
why: Selling to any buyer is free trade. Under mercantilism, the home country controls colonial trade for its own benefit.
An elected assembly is an example of self-government, not an economic system.
Mercantilism depends on trade with the home country. A colony that bans all trade sends no raw materials home.
check.hint: Follow the goods. Where must the raw materials go, and where do finished goods come from?
check.explain: Under mercantilism, raw materials (lumber) go to the home country and the colony buys the home country's finished goods (tools). The free-trade option is the opposite: the colony chooses its buyer. The elected assembly is about government, not trade.

screens.title: Why Britain Began Taxing the Colonies
screens.html:
From 1754 to 1763 Britain fought France in North America in the French and Indian War. Britain won and took control of most French land east of the Mississippi River, but the war left Britain deeply in debt.

British leaders reasoned that the colonists had been protected by the war and should help pay for it. So Parliament acted:

  • Proclamation of 1763: banned colonial settlement west of the Appalachian Mountains, partly to avoid costly wars with Native nations.
  • Stamp Act (1765): taxed newspapers, legal documents, and other printed paper.
  • Townshend Acts (1767): taxed imported glass, paper, paint, and tea.

To Britain, these were fair ways to share costs. To many colonists, they were a threat to their rights.

check.prompt:
Which war left Britain in debt and led Parliament to begin taxing the colonies? Type the name of the war.

The War

mistakes.why: The Revolutionary War came after the taxes (it began in 1775). A cause must come first: look for the war that ended in 1763.
The War of 1812 came almost fifty years later. The taxes began in the 1760s, right after the war that ended in 1763.

check.hint: Look for the war that ended in 1763, just before the new taxes began.
check.explain: The French and Indian War (1754–1763) left Britain in debt. Parliament then taxed the colonies, beginning with the Stamp Act in 1765. (In Europe this conflict was part of the Seven Years' War.)

screens.title: "No Taxation Without Representation"
screens.html:
The colonists did not mainly object to the size of the new taxes. They objected to who passed them. Colonists elected their own assemblies, such as the House of Burgesses, but they elected no one to Parliament in London. So, they argued, Parliament had no right to tax them. Their slogan was "No taxation without representation."

In 1765 delegates from nine colonies met as the Stamp Act Congress. They declared that colonists were loyal subjects of the king, but that "no taxes ever have been or can be constitutionally imposed on them but by their respective legislatures," meaning each colony's own elected assembly.

Colonists also boycotted British goods. British merchants lost money, and Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766, though it insisted it still had full power over the colonies.

check.prompt: A colonist in 1765 says, "We are loyal to King George, but only our own assembly may tax us." Which statement best explains this point of view?
options: Taxes require the consent of representatives the people themselves elect.
The colonies should break away from Britain and form a new nation.
Parliament may tax the colonies if it keeps the tax rates low.
Colonists should be given seats in the House of Commons in London.
why: The colonist says "we are loyal to King George." In 1765 most colonists wanted their rights as British subjects, not independence.
The objection is about consent, not the amount. Even a small tax passed without their representatives was unacceptable.
The Stamp Act Congress said colonists could not practically be represented in Parliament. The colonist wants the colony’s own assembly to tax, not seats in London.
check.hint: Is the colonist rejecting the king, or rejecting something narrower?
check.explain: The colonist is loyal to the king but says only "our own assembly" may tax. That is the principle of consent: people should be taxed only by representatives they elect. Independence came eleven years later. The low-tax option misses the point, because the complaint was about who taxed, not how much.

screens.title: From Protest to War to Independence
screens.html:
Each British action brought a colonial protest, and each protest brought a harsher response.

YearEvent
1770Boston Massacre: British soldiers kill five colonists
1773Boston Tea Party: colonists dump British tea into the harbor
1774Coercive Acts close Boston Harbor; First Continental Congress meets
1775Fighting at Lexington and Concord
1776Declaration of Independence, July 4
1777–1778Victory at Saratoga; France becomes an ally
1781British surrender at Yorktown
1783Treaty of Paris recognizes independence

example.prompt: Which came first, the Boston Tea Party or the Coercive Acts? Which caused the other?
steps: Find the dates: Tea Party, 1773; Coercive Acts, 1774.
The earlier event is the cause. The Coercive Acts closed the very harbor where the tea was dumped.
example.answer: The Tea Party came first. Britain passed the Coercive Acts to punish Boston for it.

check.prompt:
Complete the statement.

The American victory at {{0}} in 1777 convinced {{1}} to sign an alliance with the United States in 1778.

options: Saratoga
Yorktown
Lexington and Concord
Boston
why: Yorktown (1781) came after the alliance. French troops and ships helped win it, so it could not have caused the alliance.
Lexington and Concord (1775) began the war two years earlier. The 1777 victory that convinced an ally the Americans could win came later.
The Boston Tea Party and Boston Massacre were protests and clashes, not a 1777 battlefield victory.

options: France
Spain
Great Britain
Mexico
why: Spain did later go to war with Britain, but the 1778 treaty of alliance with the United States was signed by France.
Great Britain was the enemy the Americans were fighting.
Mexico was still a Spanish colony in 1778, not an independent country that could sign alliances.

check.hint: The cause must come before 1778. Which victory happened in 1777?
check.explain: Blank 1: Saratoga. The win at Saratoga in 1777 showed the Americans could defeat a British army. Blank 2: France. France signed an alliance in 1778 and sent money, troops, and ships. Yorktown is the tempting wrong answer, but it came in 1781, after the alliance.

screens.title: The Early Republic: From the Articles to the Constitution
screens.html:
The first plan of national government was the Articles of Confederation, in effect from 1781. The states feared a powerful central government after their experience with Britain, so they made Congress weak on purpose. Under the Articles, Congress:

  • could not collect taxes, only ask the states for money
  • could not regulate trade between the states
  • had no national courts and no president to enforce laws

In 1786–1787 Massachusetts farmers, many of them veterans facing debt and the loss of their farms, rose up in Shays' Rebellion. Congress could not raise money to help put it down. Many leaders concluded that the nation needed a stronger government. In 1787 delegates met in Philadelphia and wrote the Constitution, which replaced the Articles in 1789.

check.prompt: Why did Shays' Rebellion lead many leaders to support writing a new constitution?
options: It showed that the national government under the Articles was too weak to keep order.
It showed that the national government under the Articles had too much power over farmers.
It forced Great Britain to sign the Treaty of Paris and recognize independence.
It proved that the states should leave the Union and become separate nations.
why: This reverses the problem. The Articles government was too weak, not too strong; it could not even raise money to respond to the uprising.
The Treaty of Paris was signed in 1783, before Shays’ Rebellion (1786–1787). An effect cannot come before its cause.
Leaders drew the opposite lesson: they wanted a stronger Union, not a breakup.
check.hint: Was the problem that the government was too strong or too weak?
check.explain: Congress under the Articles could not raise money or enforce order, so it could not respond to the rebellion. That weakness convinced leaders to write a stronger Constitution in 1787. The Treaty of Paris option fails the date test: 1783 came before the rebellion.

screens.title: Washington's Precedents and Farewell Address
screens.html:
George Washington became the first president in 1789. Almost everything he did set a precedent, an example later leaders followed. He created a cabinet of advisers and stepped down after two terms, a tradition that lasted until 1940 and became law with the Twenty-second Amendment.

Disagreements in his cabinet between Alexander Hamilton (a strong national government) and Thomas Jefferson (more power for states and farmers) produced the first political parties: the Federalists and the Democratic-Republicans.

In his Farewell Address (1796), Washington gave two warnings. He warned against the "spirit of party," especially parties based on region. And on foreign policy he advised:

"The great rule of conduct for us in regard to foreign nations is in extending our commercial relations, to have with them as little political connection as possible."

check.prompt: In the quotation in the box, what does Washington advise?
options: Expand trade with other nations but keep political ties with them to a minimum
Stop trading with other nations so the country can avoid all foreign conflicts
Form political alliances with nations that are the country’s best trade partners
Let Congress, not the president, decide all questions of trade with foreign nations
why: "Extending our commercial relations" means increasing trade, not ending it. Washington wanted more trade, not less.
This reverses the second half: "as little political connection as possible" means avoid political ties, even with trade partners.
The quotation does not mention Congress or the president. It is about what kind of relations to have, not who decides.
check.hint: Split the sentence in two. What does he want more of, and what does he want less of?
check.explain: "Extending our commercial relations" means expanding trade. "As little political connection as possible" means avoiding alliances and political ties. The most common error is choosing "stop trading," which ignores the first half of the sentence.

screens.title: Growth and Independence: 1800–1823
screens.html:
In the election of 1800, Thomas Jefferson defeated President John Adams, and power passed peacefully from one party to another, a major test for the new republic.

In 1803 Jefferson bought the Louisiana Territory from France for $15 million. It stretched from the Mississippi River to the Rocky Mountains and roughly doubled the size of the country. Lewis and Clark explored it from 1804 to 1806.

The War of 1812 against Britain, fought partly over British interference with American ships and sailors, ended in a draw in 1815 but boosted national pride.

In 1823 President James Monroe announced the Monroe Doctrine: the Americas "are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers." In return, the United States would stay out of Europe's internal affairs.

check.prompt: What did the Monroe Doctrine tell European powers?
options: Do not create new colonies anywhere in North or South America.
Give up every colony you already hold anywhere in the Americas.
Join the United States in a permanent alliance for mutual defense.
Stop trading with the United States until it pays its war debts.
why: Monroe said "future colonization." He warned against new colonies; he did not demand that Europe give up existing ones.
A permanent alliance is the opposite of the doctrine. The United States promised to stay out of Europe’s affairs.
The doctrine is about colonies, not trade or war debts.
check.hint: Pay attention to the word "future" in the quotation.
check.explain: "Not to be considered as subjects for future colonization" means Europe should not start new colonies in the Americas. The tempting wrong answer, give up every colony, ignores the word "future."

screens.title: Manifest Destiny and Indian Removal
screens.html:
In 1845 journalist John L. O'Sullivan wrote that it was the nation's "manifest destiny" to spread across the continent. Manifest Destiny became the name for the belief that the United States was meant to stretch from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

Expansion was devastating for Native Americans. President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830. It led to the forced removal of the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw, and Seminole nations from the Southeast to lands west of the Mississippi River. In 1832 the Supreme Court ruled in Worcester v. Georgia that Georgia's laws had no force in Cherokee territory, but Jackson did not enforce the ruling. In 1838–1839 the U.S. Army forced the Cherokee west on the Trail of Tears; thousands died.

On the GED, ask who gained and who lost. Expansion meant land for settlers and the loss of homelands for Native nations.

check.prompt: Which was a direct result of the Indian Removal Act of 1830?
options: The forced relocation of southeastern Native nations to lands west of the Mississippi
The purchase of the Louisiana Territory from France for $15 million
The Supreme Court ruling that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories
The Missouri Compromise line that divided free and slave territory at 36°30′
why: The Louisiana Purchase happened in 1803, before the Indian Removal Act. A result must come after its cause.
That is the Dred Scott decision (1857), which was about slavery, not Native removal.
The Missouri Compromise (1820) came before the 1830 act and dealt with slavery, not Native nations.
check.hint: A result comes after 1830 and is about the people the law targeted.
check.explain: The Indian Removal Act led to the forced removal of the Cherokee and other southeastern nations, including the Trail of Tears (1838–1839). The other options either came earlier (Louisiana, 1803; Missouri Compromise, 1820) or concern slavery (Dred Scott).

screens.title: Reading a Table: How the Nation Grew
screens.html:
GED questions often give you a table and ask you to calculate or compare. Read the title, the column headings, and the units first.

AdditionYearFromArea (thousand sq. mi.)
Louisiana Purchase1803France828
Florida1819Spain72
Texas1845Republic of Texas389
Oregon Country1846Great Britain286
Mexican Cession1848Mexico529
Gadsden Purchase1853Mexico30

The units are thousands of square miles, so 828 means about 828,000 square miles. Texas was annexed in 1845; the dispute over its border helped start the Mexican-American War (1846–1848), which ended with the Mexican Cession, including California.

example.prompt: How many thousand square miles did the United States gain from Mexico in all?
steps: Find every row with Mexico in the "From" column: Mexican Cession (529) and Gadsden Purchase (30).

check.prompt: Using the table, how many thousand square miles larger was the Louisiana Purchase than the Oregon Country?

mistakes.why: You added the two areas (828 + 286). "How many larger" asks for the difference, so subtract: 828 − 286.
You subtracted the Texas area (828 − 389). Check that you are using the Oregon Country row: 286.

check.hint: "How many larger" means subtract the smaller area from the larger one.

screens.title: Sectionalism: North vs. South
screens.html:
Sectionalism is loyalty to your own region over loyalty to the nation as a whole. By the 1820s the North and the South were growing apart.

North

  • Factories, cities, railroads
  • Free labor and many immigrants
  • Growing population: more seats in the House

South

  • Plantation farming, especially cotton
  • About 4 million enslaved people by 1860
  • Equal Senate power as long as slave states = free states

Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) made cleaning cotton much faster, so cotton growing spread across the South and the demand for enslaved labor grew. In 1819 the Union had 11 free states and 11 slave states. When Missouri asked to join as a slave state, Congress passed the Missouri Compromise (1820): Missouri entered as a slave state, Maine as a free state, and slavery was banned in the rest of the Louisiana Territory north of 36°30′.

check.prompt: Why did Congress admit Maine as a free state at the same time Missouri entered as a slave state?
options: To keep an equal number of free and slave states, so neither section controlled the Senate
To end slavery in Missouri gradually by surrounding it with free states on every side
To reward the North for winning the War of 1812 against Great Britain
To give the North a majority in the Senate so it could abolish slavery
why: Missouri entered as a slave state; the compromise did not end slavery there. Maine is in New England, far from Missouri.
The compromise had nothing to do with rewarding a section for the War of 1812, which ended in a draw.
Pairing the states kept the Senate tied at 12 free and 12 slave states. It did not give the North a majority.
check.hint: Count the free and slave states before and after.
check.explain: With 11 free and 11 slave states, the Senate was balanced. Missouri alone would have made it 12 slave to 11 free. Adding Maine made it 12 to 12, so each section kept 24 senators. The "North majority" option is the most tempting, but the whole point was to keep a tie.

screens.title: The Compromises That Failed
screens.html:
The Mexican Cession reopened the fight. Each attempt to settle the slavery question made it worse.

YearEventWhat it did
1850Compromise of 1850California entered as a free state; a stricter Fugitive Slave Act forced Northerners to help capture people who had escaped slavery
1854Kansas-Nebraska ActLet settlers vote on slavery (popular sovereignty), undoing the Missouri line there; violence in "Bleeding Kansas"
1857Dred Scott v. SandfordSupreme Court: Congress cannot ban slavery in the territories; Black Americans are not citizens
1859John Brown's raidAbolitionist attack on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia

Opponents of slavery's spread formed the Republican Party in 1854. Abolitionists such as Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery, and Harriet Tubman worked to end slavery altogether.

check.prompt: Drag each event into the correct position, from earliest (1st) to latest (4th).
check.why: The most common mistake is placing the Kansas-Nebraska Act before the Compromise of 1850. Remember: 1850 California, 1854 Kansas, 1857 the Court.
check.hint: Two events have years in their names. Place them first.
check.explain: Missouri Compromise (1820) → Compromise of 1850 → Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) → Dred Scott decision (1857). Each one moved the decision about slavery in new land: first Congress drew a line, then settlers voted, then the Court said Congress could not ban it at all.

screens.title: Secession and the Start of the War
screens.html:
In the election of 1860, the Democratic Party split into Northern and Southern wings. Abraham Lincoln, the Republican candidate, won with about 40 percent of the popular vote and a majority of the electoral votes, all from free states. Lincoln promised not to touch slavery where it already existed, but he opposed its spread into the territories.

Many white Southerners believed slavery's future was now in danger. In December 1860 South Carolina seceded, meaning it formally left the Union. By February 1861 seven states had formed the Confederate States of America. On April 12, 1861, Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter, a U.S. fort in Charleston Harbor, and the war began. Four more states then joined the Confederacy, for eleven in all. Four slave states, Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, and Missouri, stayed in the Union and were called the border states.

check.prompt: Which event most directly led South Carolina to secede in December 1860?
options: The election of Abraham Lincoln as president
The Confederate attack on Fort Sumter
The signing of the Emancipation Proclamation
The surrender of the Confederate army at Appomattox
why: Fort Sumter was attacked in April 1861, months after South Carolina seceded. An effect cannot come before its cause.
The Emancipation Proclamation took effect in 1863, more than two years after secession.
Appomattox (1865) ended the war; it could not cause an event in 1860.
check.hint: Anchor the date: December 1860. Which event happened just before it?
check.explain: South Carolina seceded in December 1860, weeks after Lincoln, who opposed the spread of slavery, won the November election. Fort Sumter is the tempting answer, but it came in April 1861, after secession. Anchor the date and the other choices fall away.

screens.title: Emancipation and the End of Slavery
screens.html:
At first Lincoln's goal was to save the Union. As the war went on, ending slavery became a war aim. After the Union victory at Antietam in 1862, Lincoln announced the Emancipation Proclamation, which took effect on January 1, 1863. It:

  • declared free all enslaved people in areas in rebellion against the United States
  • did not apply to the loyal border states or to Union-held areas
  • allowed Black men to join the Union army and navy; about 180,000 served in the army

In July 1863 Union victories at Gettysburg and Vicksburg turned the war. In November, Lincoln's Gettysburg Address called for "a new birth of freedom." General Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865. The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865, abolished slavery throughout the United States.

check.prompt: Which statements about the Emancipation Proclamation are accurate? Select two answers.
options: It applied to areas that were in rebellion against the United States.
It allowed Black men to serve in the Union army and navy.
It ended slavery in Kentucky and the other loyal border states.
It was a constitutional amendment ratified by the states.
It ended the Civil War by bringing about the Confederate surrender.
why: The border states were not in rebellion, so the Proclamation did not apply to them. Slavery there ended with the Thirteenth Amendment.
The Proclamation was an executive order issued by Lincoln as commander in chief. The Thirteenth Amendment was the constitutional change.
The war went on for more than two years after the Proclamation; Lee surrendered in April 1865.
check.hint: Was the Proclamation an order from Lincoln or a change to the Constitution? Where did it apply?
check.explain: The Proclamation freed enslaved people only in areas in rebellion and opened the Union army and navy to Black men. It did not cover the border states, it was not an amendment (the Thirteenth Amendment was), and it did not end the war.

screens.title: Reading Civil War Data
screens.html:
The North had big advantages in people and industry. The South had advantages too: it fought mostly on its own land, it had experienced military leaders, and it only had to defend itself, not conquer the North.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Anchor the date: causes come before effects.
  • Colonial era: Jamestown (1607); House of Burgesses and first enslaved Africans (1619); Mayflower Compact (1620); three regions; mercantilism.
  • Revolution: French and Indian War debt → Stamp Act (1765) → "no taxation without representation" → Tea Party (1773) → Coercive Acts (1774) → Lexington and Concord (1775) → Declaration (1776) → Saratoga → French alliance → Yorktown (1781) → Treaty of Paris (1783).
  • Early republic: weak Articles → Shays' Rebellion → Constitution (1787). Washington: two terms, cabinet, trade but no permanent alliances. Louisiana Purchase (1803). Monroe Doctrine (1823): no new European colonies.
  • Expansion: Manifest Destiny; Indian Removal Act (1830) and Trail of Tears; Texas, Oregon, Mexican Cession. Every new territory raised the slavery question.
  • Sectionalism: Missouri Compromise (1820), Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), Dred Scott (1857), Lincoln elected (1860).
  • Civil War: Fort Sumter (1861); Emancipation Proclamation (1863, rebelling areas only); Gettysburg and Vicksburg (1863); Appomattox (1865); Thirteenth Amendment (1865) ended slavery everywhere.

Next: the Practice set. Read every explanation, even on questions you get right.

stimuli.title: Document 1: The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639)
stimuli.html:
Background: In 1639 the settlers of three towns along the Connecticut River adopted a written plan of government. It is often called the first written constitution in the English colonies.

…we the inhabitants and residents of Windsor, Hartford, and Wethersfield… do therefore associate and conjoin ourselves to be as one public state or commonwealth… as also in our civil affairs to be guided and governed according to such laws, rules, orders, and decrees as shall be made, ordered, and decreed as followeth:

1. It is ordered, sentenced, and decreed, that there shall be yearly two general assemblies or courts… the first shall be called the Court of Election, wherein shall be yearly chosen from time to time so many magistrates and other public officers as shall be found requisite: whereof one to be chosen governor for the year ensuing and until another be chosen, and no other magistrate to be chosen for more than one year… which choice shall be made by all that are admitted freemen and have taken the oath of fidelity…

Word help: conjoin = join together; commonwealth = a community governed for the common good; requisite = needed; freemen = adult men admitted as voting members of the colony.
stimuli.source: Fundamental Orders of Connecticut, adopted January 14, 1639 (spelling and capitalization modernized)

stimuli.title: Document 2: Resolutions of the Stamp Act Congress (1765)
stimuli.html:
1st. That His Majesty's subjects in these colonies owe the same allegiance to the crown of Great Britain that is owing from his subjects born within the realm, and all due subordination to that august body, the Parliament of Great Britain.

…

3d. That it is inseparably essential to the freedom of a people, and the undoubted rights of Englishmen, that no taxes should be imposed on them, but with their own consent, given personally, or by their representatives.

4th. That the people of these colonies are not, and from their local circumstances cannot be, represented in the House of Commons in Great Britain.

5th. That the only representatives of the people of these colonies are persons chosen therein, by themselves; and that no taxes ever have been or can be constitutionally imposed on them but by their respective legislatures.

Word help: allegiance = loyalty; subordination = being under the authority of; respective legislatures = each colony's own elected assembly.
stimuli.source: Resolutions adopted by the Stamp Act Congress, New York, October 19, 1765

stimuli.title: Document 3: Two Statements on Foreign Policy
stimuli.html:
A. President George Washington, Farewell Address (1796)

The great rule of conduct for us in regard to foreign nations is in extending our commercial relations, to have with them as little political connection as possible.… It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world…

B. President James Monroe, Annual Message to Congress (1823)

…the American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers.…

Our policy in regard to Europe… remains the same, which is, not to interfere in the internal concerns of any of its powers…

It is impossible that the allied powers should extend their political system to any portion of either continent without endangering our peace and happiness…

Word help: commercial relations = trade; allied powers = the European monarchies that had joined together after 1815; either continent = North or South America.
stimuli.source: George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796; James Monroe, Seventh Annual Message to Congress, December 2, 1823 (the Monroe Doctrine)

stimuli.title: Document 4: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)
stimuli.html:
Background: Dred Scott was an enslaved man whose enslaver, an army doctor, had taken him to live in the free state of Illinois and in part of the Wisconsin Territory where the Missouri Compromise (1820) banned slavery. Scott later sued for his freedom. In 1857 the Supreme Court ruled against him, 7 to 2. Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote the opinion of the Court.

Upon these considerations, it is the opinion of the court that the act of Congress which prohibited a citizen from holding and owning property of this kind in the territory of the United States north of the line therein mentioned is not warranted by the Constitution, and is therefore void, and that neither Dred Scott himself nor any of his family were made free by being carried into this territory, even if they had been carried there by the owner with the intention of becoming a permanent resident…

Word help: property of this kind = enslaved people; the line therein mentioned = the 36°30′ line set by the Missouri Compromise; not warranted by = not allowed by; void = having no legal force.
stimuli.source: Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 U.S. 393 (1857), opinion of the Court by Chief Justice Roger B. Taney

stimuli.title: Reading: The Cherokee and Indian Removal
stimuli.html:
[1] By the late 1820s the Cherokee Nation in Georgia had a written constitution, a newspaper printed in both English and Cherokee, and many farms, mills, and schools. [2] After gold was discovered on Cherokee land in 1829, the state of Georgia passed laws claiming authority over Cherokee territory.

[3] In 1830 Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, which President Andrew Jackson strongly supported. The law allowed the president to exchange land west of the Mississippi River for Native lands in the East. [4] The Cherokee fought removal in court. In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice John Marshall, ruled that Georgia's laws had no force inside Cherokee territory.

[5] President Jackson did not act to enforce the decision, and Georgia ignored it. [6] In 1835 a small group of Cherokee, acting without the approval of the Cherokee government, signed the Treaty of New Echota, which gave up the nation's land in the East. [7] In 1838 U.S. troops forced about 16,000 Cherokee from their homes. Thousands died on the journey west, which became known as the Trail of Tears.

stimuli.title: Document 1: The Mayflower Compact (1620)
stimuli.html:
Background: Before landing at Plymouth in 1620, the adult men aboard the Mayflower signed an agreement about how their settlement would be governed.

…Having undertaken, for the glory of God and advancement of the Christian faith and honor of our king and country, a voyage to plant the first colony in the northern parts of Virginia, do by these presents solemnly and mutually in the presence of God, and one of another, covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic, for our better ordering and preservation… and by virtue hereof to enact, constitute, and frame such just and equal laws, ordinances, acts, constitutions, and offices, from time to time, as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the colony, unto which we promise all due submission and obedience.

Word help: covenant = make a solemn agreement; civil body politic = an organized community with a government; enact = make into law; meet = suitable; submission = obeying.
stimuli.source: Mayflower Compact, November 11, 1620 (spelling modernized)

stimuli.title: Document 2: Declaration and Resolves of the First Continental Congress (1774)
stimuli.html:
Background: In 1774, after Parliament passed the Coercive Acts, delegates from twelve colonies met in Philadelphia as the First Continental Congress.

Resolved… 1. That they are entitled to life, liberty and property: and they have never ceded to any foreign power whatever, a right to dispose of either without their consent.

…4. That the foundation of English liberty, and of all free government, is a right in the people to participate in their legislative council: and as the English colonists are not represented, and from their local and other circumstances, cannot properly be represented in the British parliament, they are entitled to a free and exclusive power of legislation in their several provincial legislatures, where their right of representation can alone be preserved, in all cases of taxation and internal polity, subject only to the negative of their sovereign…

Word help: ceded = given up; dispose of = take or use; legislative council = lawmaking body; provincial legislatures = each colony's own assembly; internal polity = local government matters; negative of their sovereign = the king's veto.
stimuli.source: Declaration and Resolves of the First Continental Congress, October 14, 1774

stimuli.title: Document 3: Two Presidents on Parties and Foreign Policy
stimuli.html:
A. President George Washington, Farewell Address (1796)

I have already intimated to you the danger of parties in the State, with particular reference to the founding of them on geographical discriminations. Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally.

B. President Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address (1801)

…every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle. We have called by different names brethren of the same principle. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists.…

…peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none…

Background: Jefferson, a Democratic-Republican, had just defeated President John Adams, a Federalist, in a bitter election. Word help: intimated = hinted; geographical discriminations = divisions by region; baneful = harmful; brethren = brothers; commerce = trade; entangling = trapping, hard to escape.
stimuli.source: George Washington, Farewell Address, September 19, 1796; Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1801

…by virtue of the power in me vested as Commander-in-Chief, of the Army and Navy of the United States in time of actual armed rebellion against the authority and government of the United States, and as a fit and necessary war measure for suppressing said rebellion…
